title: Yudhiṣṭhira replies to Draupadī
voice: Yudhiṣṭhira answers Draupadī in the forest debate.
summary: Draupadī has asked why good conduct has brought them so much pain. Yudhiṣṭhira says he gives because giving is called for. For him, the chance of gaining a reward is irrelevant to the choice.
aftermath: The reply gives his reason for acting without guaranteed success. It leaves Draupadī’s question about the unequal distribution of suffering open.

title: Bhīma asks Kṛṣṇa to speak gently
voice: Bhīma advises Kṛṣṇa before the peace embassy leaves.
summary: Bhīma asks the envoy to seek peace and avoid threatening war. He expects Duryodhana to be slow to change his mind, so he urges Kṛṣṇa to try persuasion.
aftermath: The proposal shows a warrior arguing for restraint before the assembly hears the embassy. The court’s answer has yet to be given.

title: The oath-bound fighters draw Arjuna away
voice: Sañjaya describes the deployment. Arjuna speaks to Kṛṣṇa as he approaches.
summary: The oath-bound fighters arrange their chariots in a half-moon and cheer as Arjuna comes toward them. Arjuna recognizes the Trigartas and advances on their line.
aftermath: The challenge draws Arjuna into a separate fight while Droṇa presses the main army. This is the narrative opening marker used for day 12.

title: Gāndhārī surveys the battlefield
voice: Vaiśampāyana describes what Gāndhārī is able to see.
summary: The narrative gives Gāndhārī a sight that brings the distant battlefield close. Sañjaya’s account of combat gives way to a mother looking at the bodies left behind.
aftermath: Her survey prepares the laments that name the dead and speak of what victory cost their families.

title: When can a ruler oppose an ally?
voice: Bhīṣma advises Yudhiṣṭhira and cites older examples.
summary: Bhīṣma weighs whom a ruler should reconcile with and whom to oppose. He argues that a friend or teacher who harms the kingdom can be resisted and cites King Sagara’s treatment of his own son.
aftermath: The advice places public duty in tension with private loyalty. It follows Bhīṣma’s earlier discussion of effort, fortune, and judgment.

title: Who first tells this story?
voice: Ugraśravas speaks to the sages at Śaunaka’s gathering.
summary: Ugraśravas arrives after hearing Vaiśampāyana recite Vyāsa’s narrative at Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice. The first audience asks where he has come from.
aftermath: The opening sets up two different audiences. The battles belong to the past of both tellings.

title: Devavrata’s two promises
voice: Devavrata addresses the fisherman who raised Satyavatī.
summary: Devavrata yields the succession to any child of Satyavatī. The fisherman worries about a later claim by Devavrata’s own children, so Devavrata also pledges lifelong celibacy.
aftermath: Śāntanu can marry Satyavatī. Devavrata’s arrangement outlasts his father and shapes the later struggle over succession.

title: A second Kuru capital
voice: Dhṛtarāṣṭra addresses the Pāṇḍavas.
summary: The king tells the brothers to avoid another dispute by occupying Khāṇḍavaprastha. Having received half the realm, the returning brothers establish the city named Indraprastha.
aftermath: The cousins now have distinct seats of power. Yudhiṣṭhira’s court and treasury become stakes in the next parva.

title: The first losses
voice: Yudhiṣṭhira supplies each stake and Śakuni announces each win.
summary: Yudhiṣṭhira begins this series with gold, then wagers vehicles, elephants, people in household service and other royal resources. Each declared loss leads to another stake.
aftermath: The court sees household and state resources treated as a ruler’s property. Vidura warns Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the next chapter.

title: When the stake becomes a person
voice: Śakuni presses Yudhiṣṭhira for another wager.
summary: Yudhiṣṭhira stakes his brothers in order, then himself. Śakuni tells the already defeated king to stake Draupadī to recover himself and finally declares that wager won.
aftermath: The exact order gives Draupadī the basis for challenging the court.

title: Who had authority to stake Draupadī?
voice: Draupadī questions the messenger and Bhīṣma answers in the hall.
summary: Draupadī asks whether Yudhiṣṭhira lost himself before he staked her. Bhīṣma names conflicting assumptions about property and a husband’s authority, then says he cannot decide the question.
aftermath: The hall hears the question without settling it. Vikarṇa and Karṇa take opposing positions in the next chapter.

title: Vikarṇa and Karṇa dispute the wager
voice: Vikarṇa and Karṇa address the assembled rulers.
summary: Vikarṇa argues that Draupadī remains unwon, citing the order of losses, pressure on the gambler and her marriage to all five brothers. Karṇa interprets the elders’ silence as assent and attacks Vikarṇa’s argument.
aftermath: Two Kaurava allies disagree openly. The court’s authority is itself at issue.

title: The wager of years
voice: Duryodhana and his allies appeal to Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
summary: With the brothers released, Duryodhana argues that they will retaliate and proposes another game. Its terms are twelve years in the forest and a thirteenth year without recognition.
aftermath: Any discovery in the last year would restart the forest term. The rules govern Virāṭa as well as the forest book.

title: A gathering in Dvaita forest
voice: Vaiśampāyana introduces Baka Dālbhya and Yudhiṣṭhira.
summary: Brahmins gather around the Pāṇḍavas, and the account sets the sound of their recitation beside that of bowstrings. Baka Dālbhya addresses the king among the seers.
aftermath: The exiles still have a community and interlocutors. The next chapter returns to the family’s internal debate.

title: Draupadī asks about anger
voice: Draupadī addresses Yudhiṣṭhira beside the other exiles.
summary: Draupadī recalls how Duryodhana watched the family depart. She contrasts the king’s conduct with what it has earned and challenges him over his restraint.
aftermath: Their exchange moves the harm of the dice hall into a debate about when forbearance is appropriate.

title: Does good conduct guarantee a good outcome?
voice: Draupadī replies to Yudhiṣṭhira.
summary: Draupadī knows duty matters more to Yudhiṣṭhira than kingdom or family. His undeserved suffering makes her question how wealth and distress are actually distributed.
aftermath: Her challenge makes an argument about consequences. Yudhiṣṭhira then explains why he continues to act from duty.

title: Why tell Yudhiṣṭhira about Nala?
voice: Bṛhadaśva begins a tale for the exiled Yudhiṣṭhira.
summary: The sage introduces Nala, king of Niṣadha, and Damayantī, a princess of Vidarbha. Their virtues and the report each hears about the other prepare their meeting.
aftermath: The tale has its own setting and time. It answers the anxieties of a king who has also lost a kingdom at dice.

title: Sāvitrī follows Yama
voice: Mārkaṇḍeya recounts the scene to Yudhiṣṭhira.
summary: Satyavān grows weak as he chops wood. Sāvitrī supports him as he sinks down; the encounter with Yama turns her vigil into an extended negotiation.
aftermath: By following him she creates a chance to ask for successive boons. Mārkaṇḍeya uses the whole story to answer a question about loyalty under adversity.

title: The price of drinking first
voice: A yakṣa addresses the brothers who come to a pool.
summary: The brothers need water. A voice warns them to answer questions before drinking, but thirst and attempts to use force override the warning. Each who drinks falls.
aftermath: Yudhiṣṭhira arrives to find his brothers fallen. He must approach the demand differently in the following chapter.

title: A ruler answers the yakṣa
voice: Yudhiṣṭhira encounters the yakṣa after finding his brothers.
summary: Seeing no marks of weapons, Yudhiṣṭhira seeks a cause. He accepts questions before drinking and ultimately chooses Nakula when offered one brother, reasoning that each of his father’s wives should still have a son.
aftermath: The encounter tests judgment and fairness; its outcome protects the brothers’ chance of completing the incognito year.

title: Choosing names for the incognito year
voice: The exiles plan their roles before entering Virāṭa’s kingdom.
summary: Yudhiṣṭhira chooses to become Kaṅka, a man known to play dice. The strategy uses each person’s skills while disguising rank and kinship.
aftermath: The next chapter extends the preparations to the other roles. Their safety depends on keeping the terms of exile.

title: Choosing between Kṛṣṇa and his force
voice: Kṛṣṇa gives Arjuna first choice. Balarāma explains his own decision to Duryodhana.
summary: Kṛṣṇa offers soldiers to one side and his own unarmed presence to the other. Arjuna chooses Kṛṣṇa. Duryodhana leaves with the force, and Balarāma declines to fight for either cousin.
aftermath: Arjuna’s choice puts Kṛṣṇa beside him in the chariot when the battle starts.

title: Why can the king not sleep?
voice: Vidura counsels Dhṛtarāṣṭra at night.
summary: The king asks to hear what is right. Vidura starts by asking whether anxiety over another person’s wealth is robbing him of sleep, then turns to how wise and reckless people act.
aftermath: The exchange opens a longer series of advice on restraint and how a ruler treats family and counsel.

title: The proposal for five villages
voice: Yudhiṣṭhira tells Kṛṣṇa what settlement he can accept.
summary: Yudhiṣṭhira lays out a small territorial demand so the two groups can survive without fighting. He names four places and leaves the fifth open.
aftermath: The demand is a negotiating position. Kṛṣṇa will carry the case to a court where Duryodhana refuses to yield land.

title: Duryodhana rejects the settlement
voice: Duryodhana addresses Kṛṣṇa in the assembly.
summary: Duryodhana refuses to concede land, even the ground that a needle point would pierce. The statement makes clear how little room the envoy has to negotiate.
aftermath: The peace attempt fails. The narrative turns toward individual choices and toward armies preparing to meet.

title: Why Karṇa stays
voice: Karṇa replies to Kuntī before battle.
summary: He says changing sides now would look like fear and would abandon those depending on him. He still promises Kuntī to spare four of her sons if he can.
aftermath: Arjuna is the exception. The promise prepares their duel and gives Kuntī’s later disclosure its force.

title: Vyāsa speaks to Dhṛtarāṣṭra
voice: Vyāsa presents omens to the Kuru king.
summary: The chapter gathers troubling descriptions including the Moon and a reversal in the relation of Arundhatī to Vasiṣṭha. The signs sit together in a speech before the battle report.
aftermath: Readers can follow the star verse to Oak’s meridian interpretation while keeping the surrounding omens in view.

title: Arjuna looks at both armies
voice: Sañjaya relates what Arjuna says to Kṛṣṇa.
summary: Arjuna asks Kṛṣṇa to stop the chariot and see who is gathered. The ranks contain those he owes duties to as relatives, pupils and teachers.
aftermath: His dilemma leads into the conversation continued in the next chapter.

title: The opening in the formation
voice: Sañjaya narrates Abhimanyu’s entry.
summary: Abhimanyu breaks through in front of Droṇa. The text then describes warriors and troops surrounding him after he enters.
aftermath: The entry succeeds and exposes him to concentrated attack. It prepares the events that lead to Arjuna’s vow.

title: The teacher puts down his bow
voice: Sañjaya reports the culmination of the attack on Droṇa.
summary: The account moves from the misleading report about Droṇa’s son to his decision to cast off his weapons after Bhīma speaks. Dhṛṣṭadyumna takes the opening.
aftermath: There is horror at the manner of the attack. The final book returns to the deception as a problem for Yudhiṣṭhira.

title: Who may invoke the rules of battle?
voice: Kṛṣṇa answers Karṇa in the chariot duel.
summary: Karṇa’s wheel has sunk. Kṛṣṇa answers his appeal to dharma by recalling Draupadī in the assembly and the party that used the dice game.
aftermath: The duel ends with Karṇa’s defeat. Earlier conduct becomes part of a debate about whether to grant him protection.

title: The blow in the mace duel
voice: Sañjaya describes the duel between Bhīma and Duryodhana.
summary: The narrative recalls Bhīma’s vow to break Duryodhana’s thighs and depicts him doing so. The blow brings the contest to a close.
aftermath: The manner of victory becomes the subject of an argument over the rules of combat.

title: The attack on the sleeping camp
voice: Vaiśampāyana follows Aśvatthāman inside the camp.
summary: Aśvatthāman enters at night. His companions guard the exits while he attacks a camp whose warriors believe the day’s battle has ended.
aftermath: The war’s casualties now include people absent from its closing duel. Draupadī and the surviving brothers face a new loss.

title: Kuntī asks the brothers to mourn Karṇa
voice: Kuntī speaks to her sons while the families make water offerings.
summary: She tells the Pāṇḍavas that the man they fought as Karṇa was their elder brother. Yudhiṣṭhira asks why they learned this only after his death.
aftermath: They include their adversary in the rites. Their relationship to the dead changes in the act of mourning.

title: Effort, fortune, and trust
voice: Bhīṣma advises the new king.
summary: Bhīṣma says effort and fate both matter but asks Yudhiṣṭhira to focus on what a ruler can do. He identifies truth as a source of trust.
aftermath: The advice gives the postwar book a practical question. What should the king repeatedly do to earn trust?

title: How does duty change in a crisis?
voice: Yudhiṣṭhira describes a ruler without resources. Bhīṣma replies.
summary: The depleted king is pressed by a stronger opponent. Bhīṣma considers how the treasury and force depend on each other and when relief should follow emergency demands.
aftermath: His answer distinguishes normal conduct from a response to danger. The following chapter continues with negotiation and withdrawal.

title: When should a king give up the capital?
voice: Bhīṣma answers a renewed question about an invading ruler.
summary: He distinguishes an opponent who can be negotiated with from one whose aims make agreement harder. He weighs agreeing to terms and leaving the capital to survive.
aftermath: The chapter explores why retaining the means to rebuild can matter more than holding ground in a particular moment.

title: Can liberation wait?
voice: A father and son speak inside one of Bhīṣma’s examples.
summary: The father describes a sequence of life duties. The son argues that ageing and death can interrupt any plan that leaves the search for what is good until later.
aftermath: Bhīṣma frames a dispute in which inherited order is challenged by the urgency of time.

title: Why does an ascetic visit a merchant?
voice: Bhīṣma tells Yudhiṣṭhira about Jājali and Tulādhāra.
summary: Jājali’s ascetic self-confidence is checked when he hears that Tulādhāra is his superior in dharma. He goes to Vārāṇasī and finds the merchant selling ordinary goods.
aftermath: The encounter sets up a discussion of daily conduct and the treatment of living beings outside a life of austerity.

title: A gift that keeps yielding
voice: Yudhiṣṭhira asks Bhīṣma to weigh different gifts.
summary: Bhīṣma praises land for what it can keep producing. His examples include crops, livestock and materials that sustain a livelihood.
aftermath: The next question leads to Nārada’s praise of the immediate value of food.

title: A gift that meets a need immediately
voice: Bhīṣma passes on Nārada’s answer about food.
summary: Nārada argues that food supports householders and mendicants alike. The gift helps because their continued life depends on it.
aftermath: The nested answer makes a different case from the preceding chapter’s emphasis on the lasting yield of land.

title: The teacher waits for a turning point
voice: Bhīṣma addresses Yudhiṣṭhira and those who return to him.
summary: The chapter refers to the Sun turning north. Bhīṣma counts the nights spent lying on the arrows and names Māgha.
aftermath: The death closes his teachings. These details become data only under a specified interpretation of the count and calendar.

title: Arjuna meets the son who must oppose him
voice: Vaiśampāyana narrates the horse’s arrival in Maṇipura.
summary: Babhruvāhana greets his father Arjuna. The ritual surrounding the wandering horse gives Arjuna reason to demand a challenge, and Ulūpī urges the younger man to fight.
aftermath: Both fall in the encounter. Family ties complicate the ritual assertion of the restored king’s authority.

title: Nārada brings news from the forest
voice: Nārada reports the fire to Yudhiṣṭhira.
summary: A wind feeds a forest fire. Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gāndhārī and Kuntī remain, while Sañjaya escapes.
aftermath: The forest retreat ends in loss, and the surviving court must perform the rites for its elders.

title: Leaving Dvārakā
voice: Arjuna addresses people in the city. Vaiśampāyana tells what happens after their departure.
summary: Arjuna warns the inhabitants that the sea will cover Dvārakā and helps organize their departure. The narrative then describes the city filling with water.
aftermath: The survivors’ difficulties continue away from the city. The literary account has a separate evidentiary status from material recovered offshore.

title: A place in heaven with a condition
voice: Yudhiṣṭhira answers Indra about the dog.
summary: Indra offers passage to heaven if the dog is left behind. Yudhiṣṭhira refuses to abandon a being that has depended on him.
aftermath: The dog’s identity as Dharma turns the offer into a test. Another test follows after the ascent.

title: Indra explains the final test
voice: Indra and Dharma address Yudhiṣṭhira after he elects to stay with his kin.
summary: Indra explains the king’s experience by recalling the misleading report about Droṇa’s son. Dharma acknowledges the conduct Yudhiṣṭhira showed during the ordeal.
aftermath: The last trial ties the final judgments back to a specific wartime decision.
